transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?

I came in because I’ve had to be more in front of people at work, and I can’t stop focusing on this one part of my face that looks uneven in photos. Everyone tells me they barely notice it, but I see it every time.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your reflection in mirrors or other surfaces throughout the day to look at it?

Yeah. Before I send event photos or get on a vendor meeting, I keep checking my face in my phone camera. I’ll retake pictures, tilt my head different ways, or ask a coworker if I look weird. It can take up enough time that I get behind on the planning work.

When you feel uncomfortable being in front of people at work, is that entirely because of your concern about your face, or do you also worry about other things like saying the wrong thing or embarrassing yourself?
It’s really because of my face. Since I’ve had to be more visible at work, I keep looking at that uneven part in photos, and I can’t let it go, even though other people say they barely notice it.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F40.1 as social anxiety is solely driven by appearance concerns, and F42 as obsessions/compulsions are restricted to perceived appearance defect (ICD-10 dysmorphophobia/BDD under F45.2).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with a perceived physical defect (facial unevenness in photos) that is barely noticeable or unobserved by others. This is accompanied by repetitive, time-consuming checking behaviors (checking phone camera, retaking photos, seeking reassurance) leading to occupational impairment. Social discomfort is solely attributable to appearance concerns rather than a generalized fear of social scrutiny, fitting body dysmorphic disorder classified under ICD-10 F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder).
